rows.title: Adam (Achitteronose)
rows.summary: Adam, also identified as Achitteronose, was a seventeenth-century western Long Island and Massapequa-associated bilingual envoy.
rows.why_this_matters: Adam's record shows that Native diplomacy depended on people who could work across languages, communities, and colonial governments. His story preserves western Long Island Native agency in communication, treaty-making, and land negotiation during a period of intense pressure.
rows.activity_update_summary: Newly featured: Adam's documented role as a bilingual envoy in the fall 1655 Rockaway Neck deed negotiations and his participation in the March 1656 mutual-protection treaty at Hempstead.

rows.title: Algonquian Language and Place Names
rows.summary: Native Long Island place names preserve source-attributed interpretations connected with water, land, ecology, community memory, spelling variation, and present-day language continuity.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added 3 public education questions with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Alice Osceola Bunn Martinez
rows.summary: Alice Osceola Bunn Martinez (1901–1992) was a Shinnecock craftworker, trading-post founder, family historian, and oral-history contributor.
rows.why_this_matters: Alice Bunn Martinez's record shows how craft knowledge, Native-owned commerce, education, and oral history could reinforce one another. Her work helped sustain a family economy while preserving details of Shinnecock working life that later histories might otherwise have lost.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Shinnecock craftworker, trading-post founder, family historian, and oral-history contributor Alice Osceola Bunn Martinez with three distinct Historic Moments.

rows.title: Anthony Beaman (Chief Running Bull)
rows.summary: Anthony Beaman (1879–1963), also documented as Chief Running Bull and Anthony “Did” Beaman, was a Shinnecock medicine man and cultural participant whose story connects family history, botanical knowledge, and public pageant records.
rows.why_this_matters: Anthony Beaman’s surviving record keeps a named Shinnecock knowledge keeper visible across family history, plant lore, and twentieth-century public memory while showing the care needed when captions and later compilations provide only part of a life.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Anthony Beaman (Chief Running Bull) with family history, documented knowledge, pageant records, and three linked Historic Moments.

rows.title: Archaic Period (3,500 – 1,300 B.C.)
rows.summary: The Archaic Period ( 3,500- 1,300 B.C. ) is identified by semi-nomadic village settlements that were usually located near tidal bays where they could harvest shellfish. In the winter months, some of the households probably moved into sheltered areas where trees or low hills protected them from the cold winter winds.

rows.title: Beach Plum
rows.summary: Beach plum is a hardy coastal shrub associated with Plum Island, dune landscapes, and seasonal foodways around Long Island's bays and beaches.

rows.title: Betty Lewis Cromwell (Shinnecock)
rows.summary: Betty Lewis Cromwell was a Shinnecock community member documented in a photograph caption from a December 6, 1997 Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum fundraiser.
rows.why_this_matters: Betty Lewis Cromwell shows why community photographs, fundraiser records, and museum history matter. Even a brief source mention can help keep Shinnecock women visible in public memory when handled carefully and without inventing unsupported biography.

rows.title: Building Respectful Institutional Relationships
rows.summary: Guidance for schools, museums, towns, and preservation groups building accountable relationships with Native Nations.
rows.why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Published a new public education guide with 1 source-based answer.

rows.title: Burial
rows.summary: Burial traditions on Long Island span ancient, colonial, and contemporary contexts, including archaeological evidence, historic descriptions, and continuing responsibilities to protect the dead.

rows.title: Burial Protection and Sacred Landscapes
rows.summary: Burial places, ancestral remains, and sacred landscapes require respect, legal protection, and careful suppression of exact locations.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added 7 public education questions with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Central Long Island Native Communities
rows.summary: A regional overview for Setauket/Setalcott, Secatogue, Nissequogue, Unkechaug, Yaphank, Wading River, and neighboring central Long Island communities.

rows.title: Charles Martinez
rows.summary: Charles Martinez was a Chiricahua Apache Hampton Institute graduate, animal-husbandry worker, golf-club foreman, mechanic, and member of the Martinez family craft economy at Shinnecock.
rows.why_this_matters: Charles Martinez's surviving record connects off-reservation education with work, family, and Native enterprise at Shinnecock. Keeping the gaps in his dates and lineage visible makes the biography more useful: it presents what the sources establish without turning family memory into an unsupported genealogy.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a date-cautious biography of Chiricahua Apache Hampton Institute graduate, golf-club foreman, mechanic, and Shinnecock community family member Charles Martinez.

rows.title: Charles Sumner Bunn
rows.summary: Charles Sumner Bunn (1865–1952) was a Shinnecock decoy carver, guide, church elder, trustee, and historical witness whose public life joined creative work, community governance, and land memory.
rows.why_this_matters: Charles Sumner Bunn’s life brings artistic labor, community leadership, and legal memory into one story. His decoys and guiding work supported a household, while his trustee service, 1935 voting-rights motion, and later boundary testimony show how cultural knowledge and civic action remained connected across generations.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Shinnecock carver and guide Charles Sumner Bunn with four linked Historic Moments, a public-location chronology, trustee and church service, the 1935 voting-rights motion, and his 1952 boundary testimony.

rows.title: Chief Harry Wallace of the Unkechaug
rows.summary: Chief Harry Wallace, also written Harry B. Wallace in some sources, is an Unkechaug leader, attorney, and advocate for sovereignty, language, community renewal, and Poospatuck Reservation life.
rows.why_this_matters: Chief Wallace shows contemporary Indigenous sovereignty on Long Island. His biography connects governance, language revitalization, legal advocacy, community renewal, and continued Unkechaug life at Poospatuck.

rows.title: Chief Mahue / Mayhew of Unkechaug
rows.summary: Mahue, also written Mahew, Mayhew, or John Mahue, was an Unkechaug and Setauket-connected proprietor, headman, and negotiator in seventeenth-century records. His name appears in land and testimony records that show Native authority, community representation, and diplomacy in the Brookhaven and Moriches area.
rows.why_this_matters: Mahue shows Unkechaug leadership in land, kinship, and community survival records. His biography connects Setauket, Moriches, Watchogue, and Poospatuck histories without reducing him to a single colonial title.

rows.title: Chief Robert Pharaoh
rows.summary: Robert Pharaoh was a Montaukett leader whose work connected burial-ground protection, cultural education, community governance, museum development, traditional agriculture, and federal acknowledgment.
rows.why_this_matters: Robert Pharaoh’s work connects preservation, cultural teaching, governance, and federal acknowledgment as related parts of modern Montaukett sovereignty, while preserving the complexity of internal leadership debates.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Chief Robert Pharaoh with burial-ground protection, cultural education, governance, preservation, federal acknowledgment work, and mapped Historic Moments.

rows.title: Cockenoe (de Long Island)
rows.summary: Cockenoe, also written Cockenow, Cheekanoo, Chekkonnow, Cheknow, and Chegonoe, was a seventeenth-century Long Island Algonquian interpreter, translator, diplomat, and boundary worker. Sources connect him with language work, deed interpretation, and Native diplomacy across Long Island and southern New England.
rows.why_this_matters: Cockenoe places Native language knowledge and diplomacy at the center of Long Island history. His work as an interpreter and boundary negotiator shaped records that colonial governments later used to claim land, making careful interpretation essential.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added Lois Marie Hunter's page-level 1950 account to Cockenoe while retaining John Strong for the separate 1657 Hempstead conference moment.

rows.title: Colonial Descriptions of Indians
rows.summary: Early written descriptions of Indigenous Long Islanders often come from colonial officials, missionaries, local historians, museum workers, and outside researchers. These sources can preserve names, events, places, and testimony, but they also carry racism, Christian judgment, vanishing-race myths, and outsider assumptions about Native identity.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Continued Indigenous Presence Today
rows.summary: Native continuity on Long Island includes governance, recognition, cultural revitalization, stewardship, family networks, and living community presence.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Creation of Long Island
rows.summary: Long Island's glacial formation shaped waterways, shorelines, travel routes, and homelands later used by Algonquian-speaking communities.

rows.title: David Fowler (Montaukett)
rows.summary: David Fowler (1735–1807) was a Montaukett teacher, traveler, community organizer, and political leader whose work connected Montauk to the Native-led Brothertown movement.
rows.why_this_matters: David Fowler’s life shows Montaukett history extending far beyond one place. His teaching, long-distance service, family responsibilities, and Brothertown leadership reveal Native people using education, kinship, movement, and government to sustain community under colonial land pressure.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Montaukett organizer David Fowler with a six-stop life chronology, six linked Historic Moments, and an identity note separating him from a later namesake.

rows.title: Dog
rows.summary: Dogs have long been part of Indigenous life on Long Island as companions, household protectors, village animals, and beings with spiritual meaning. Early records show Native communities defending their dogs when colonial authorities tried to restrict or kill them.
rows.why_this_matters: Dogs are part of Indigenous Long Island history through everyday life: homes, safety, companionship, spirit, and colonial interference. Colonial records about dogs often say as much about English control over Native households, movement, and authority as they do about animals themselves. Native families continued to keep dogs as part of home, protection, companionship, and community memory.

rows.title: Donald Treadwell (Lone Otter)
rows.summary: Donald Treadwell, also known as Lone Otter, was an Unkechaug writer, historian, healer, and community leader whose work connected Native-authored history, education, governance, and public health.
rows.why_this_matters: Donald Treadwell’s life preserves an Unkechaug account of twentieth-century schooling, writing, tribal leadership, and the practical work of improving water and health conditions at the Poospatuck Reservation.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Donald Treadwell (Lone Otter), including his writing, education, leadership, clean-water advocacy, date conflicts in the record, and linked Historic Moments.

rows.title: Early Contact Period (1600 AD – 1700 AD)
rows.summary: The early contact period on Long Island involved trade, diplomacy, land pressure, disease, violence, and changing relationships between Native communities and Europeans.

rows.title: Early Indigenous Presence / Paleoindian Period (c. 10,000-8000 BCE)
rows.summary: Rare fluted stone points connect Long Island to Indigenous life at the end of the last Ice Age while also showing how much the surviving archaeological evidence cannot answer.
rows.why_this_matters: The earliest archaeological finds extend Indigenous Long Island history beyond written records by more than ten thousand years. They also show the limits of archaeology: a few displaced stone points cannot supply a complete account of the people who made and used them.

rows.title: Eastern Long Island Native Communities
rows.summary: Eastern Long Island includes living Native nations, ancestral homelands, maritime labor histories, land claims, language survivals, and sacred landscapes. Shinnecock, Montaukett, Corchaug, Manhansett, Unkechaug, and neighboring communities belong in relation to one another, not as isolated map points.

rows.title: Ecology and Flexible Sedentism
rows.summary: Seasonal movement, estuaries, ponds, shellfish, fishing, hunting, planting, and long-term settlement patterns shaped Native Long Island life without fitting simple stereotypes.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Education at Shinnecock
rows.summary: Shinnecock education connects community teaching, the reservation school, Native educators, state responsibility, and students' continuing pursuit of learning.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a Shinnecock education article connecting the reservation school, Native teachers, the corrected 1874–1875 rebuilding chronology, and Hunter's 1950 school account.

rows.title: Eliza Fowler Beaman
rows.summary: Eliza Fowler Beaman was a storyteller, plant-knowledge contributor, Southampton schoolteacher, and public community participant whose surviving record connects Montaukett and Shinnecock histories while leaving important family details unresolved.
rows.why_this_matters: Eliza Fowler Beaman’s record preserves a woman’s own contributions to storytelling, plant knowledge, education, and public community life. Keeping the gaps and conflicting captions visible also shows how responsibly written history can honor a person without inventing a complete biography.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported profile of Eliza Fowler Beaman with her storytelling and plant-knowledge contributions, teaching role, public gatherings, and a two-stop chronology that preserves unresolved family-caption conflicts.

rows.title: Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile (Chee Chee)
rows.summary: Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile, also known as Chee Chee and Elizabeth Bess Haile, was a Shinnecock tribal member whose public life included storytelling, museum work, Tribal Council service, land-rights advocacy, and oral-history preservation.

rows.title: Elliott Alphonso Kellis
rows.summary: Elliott Alphonso Kellis (1883–1949) was a Shinnecock boarding-house owner, elected trustee, and community organizer whose public record connects Kellis Rest, land governance, Conscience Point, and a 1938 reservation powwow.
rows.why_this_matters: Elliott Alphonso Kellis’s record shows how Shinnecock public life joined economic initiative, hospitality, elected service, land governance, and community gatherings. Reading those activities together makes a long history of practical self-government visible without turning a historical title or one event into a larger claim than the sources support.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Elliott Alphonso Kellis with Kellis Rest, elected trustee service, three linked Historic Moments, and a public-location chronology that distinguishes his historical title from an elected office.

rows.title: Fall / Autumn
rows.summary: Fall was a season of harvest, storage, hunting, and preparation. Corn, beans, squash, nuts, and other foods could be gathered and processed for the colder months. Sources also describe fall and winter as important hunting seasons, when deer and other animals provided meat, hides, sinew, bone, and other materials.

rows.title: Fishing
rows.summary: Fishing history on Native Long Island connects food, technology, waterways, wampum, whaling, bay labor, and continuing community relationships with the coast.

rows.title: Food
rows.summary: Foodways on Native Long Island include shellfish, fish, plants, animals, planting, storage, seasonal movement, and contemporary stewardship rather than a single static diet.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added Hunter's Shinnecock account of corn, succotash, gathering, gardens, seafood, and women's work sustaining families and food knowledge.

rows.title: Further Learning: Indigenous Long Island
rows.summary: A starting point for books, Native-authored resources, museums, cultural centers, and continued learning.
rows.why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Published a new public education guide with 1 source-based answer.

rows.title: George Lewis Fowler Sr.
rows.summary: George Lewis Fowler Sr. (circa 1858–1931) was a Montaukett gardener, caretaker, and gondolier whose Freetown home preserves a family history of labor, dispossession, and continuity after Indian Fields.
rows.why_this_matters: George Lewis Fowler’s life shifts attention from a historic building alone to the Montaukett family who rebuilt life around it. His work and his effort to keep the Freetown house in the family show continuity, agency, and care after dispossession from Indian Fields.
rows.activity_update_summary: Clarified what the surviving sources do and do not document about Sarah Melissa Horton Fowler without creating a speculative standalone biography.

rows.title: Historic Preservation
rows.summary: Indigenous historic preservation on Long Island protects burial places, cultural landscapes, community buildings, records, and other places whose meaning continues in Native communities. New York law now establishes procedures for discoveries of unmarked human remains and funerary objects outside regulated cemeteries.
rows.why_this_matters: Preservation is not only about old buildings or objects. Native communities protect ancestors, homelands, gathering places, language, memory, and the right to decide how culturally important places are understood and cared for.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added 2 public education questions with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: History and Place Names
rows.summary: A guide to Long Island place names, variant spellings, cross-references, uncertain locations, and names that William Wallace Tooker questioned or interpreted cautiously.

rows.title: Indian Forts
rows.summary: Fortified Native places on Long Island reflect defense, diplomacy, and changing pressures before and during the seventeenth-century contact period.

rows.title: Indian Missions on Long Island
rows.summary: A short overview of Indian mission activity on Long Island, including missionaries, Native communities, and Christian mission records.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Indigenous Languages of Long Island
rows.summary: Long Island's Native languages are related but not interchangeable. Western Munsee relationships, eastern connections across Long Island Sound, colonial spellings, and present-day revitalization all require careful distinction.
rows.why_this_matters: Language carries relationships among people, land, water, memory, and community. Surviving colonial spellings preserve fragments of Indigenous speech, but they cannot replace the knowledge and authority of Native communities working to reclaim their languages.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Indigenous-Led Economic Development
rows.summary: An introduction to Native economic development as self-determination, community investment, and cultural continuity.
rows.why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Published a new public education guide with 1 source-based answer.

rows.title: Jeremiah Pharoah, Montaukett Whaler
rows.summary: Jeremiah Pharoah was a Montaukett deep-sea whaler whose life connected Indian Fields, Nantucket, Sag Harbor, Samson Occom's book history, and archaeological evidence from his household. McGovern's research connects him with whaling out of Nantucket, his 1794 marriage to Aloosa / Lois Tallman, his 1798 return to Montauk, and household material culture at Indian Fields.
rows.why_this_matters: Jeremiah Pharoah's life shows Montaukett maritime labor as global, literate, and deeply tied to family and homeland. His own recorded words, whaling history, and household material culture challenge any idea that Native Long Island history ended with colonial land loss.

rows.title: Jeremy Dennis
rows.summary: Jeremy Dennis is the Creator of On This Site and a Shinnecock Tribal Member. He is a contemporary fine art photographer whose work uses photography, mapped places, research, and public storytelling to document Native Long Island.
rows.why_this_matters: Jeremy Dennis created On This Site as a Shinnecock-led public map, photography, and research project. His biography makes the project authorship visible and connects contemporary Native presence, art, and community memory.

rows.title: John A. Strong
rows.summary: John A. Strong is a historian and ethnohistorian whose scholarship has shaped modern interpretation of Native Long Island history, especially Shinnecock, Montaukett, Unkechaug, and broader Algonquian histories of land, labor, sovereignty, and survivance.
rows.why_this_matters: John A. Strong's work interprets Native Long Island through careful historical research rather than simplified myths of disappearance. His scholarship connects places, records, families, labor, law, and community survival, placing academic history in conversation with public memory and Native-led interpretation.

rows.title: Keeossechok, Sachem of the Secatogue
rows.summary: Keeossechok was a Secatogue sachem whose clearest surviving record is the June 1, 1657 Five Necks deed for South Shore meadow lands.
rows.why_this_matters: Keeossechok matters because even sparse deed records preserve named Secatogue leadership and show that South Shore marshes, necks, and bays were Native homelands before colonial town boundaries remade the map.

rows.title: Killed Pottery
rows.summary: Killed steatite vessels appear in Orient-period burial contexts, where deliberately broken stone vessels formed part of ceremonial offerings.

rows.title: Land Deeds and Dispossession
rows.summary: Long Island land deeds were colonial records shaped by unequal power, debt, law, translation, imposed leadership categories, and Native resistance rather than simple fair sales.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added 2 public education questions with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Late Woodland Period
rows.summary: Late Woodland life on Long Island included changing settlement patterns, food cultivation, pottery, coastal harvesting, trade, and community defense.

rows.title: Learning Indigenous Words Respectfully
rows.summary: A careful guide to uncertain historical pronunciations, colonial spellings, and respectful use of community-authored language resources.
rows.why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Published a new public education guide with 2 source-based answers.

rows.title: Lois “Princess Nowedonah” Hunter
rows.summary: Lois Marie Hunter, also known as Princess Nowedonah, was a Shinnecock educator, author, public speaker, and tribal historian whose work taught Shinnecock continuity, public memory, women's advocacy, and Native self-representation in the 20th century.
rows.why_this_matters: Lois Hunter's story centers Shinnecock women's leadership, education, writing, and public advocacy. Her biography shows Native cultural authority and community knowledge in the 20th century, especially the ways Shinnecock people taught and defended their own history.
rows.activity_update_summary: Expanded Lois Hunter's biography with material from her 1950 book and stronger connections to her teaching, public history, and community work.

rows.title: Mandush, Shinnecock Sachem
rows.summary: Mandush was a Shinnecock sachem named in seventeenth-century Southampton records. His name appears among the Native signers of the December 13, 1640 Southampton deed, and later testimony remembered Mandush in relation to Shinnecock and Montaukett political authority.
rows.why_this_matters: Mandush helps show that early Southampton land history involved named Shinnecock leaders, not anonymous "Indians" in the background of colonial settlement. His record also shows why deeds and testimony must be read carefully: colonial documents preserved Native diplomacy, but through legal settings shaped by land pressure.

rows.title: Mangwobe, Sachem of Rockaway
rows.summary: Mangwobe was a mid-seventeenth-century Rockaway sachem named in the July 4, 1657 Hempstead boundary conference.
rows.why_this_matters: Mangwobe keeps Rockaway leadership visible in western Long Island land history. His brief but important record shows that Merrick, Massapequa, Rockaway, Montaukett, and Hempstead boundary questions were connected through Native diplomacy.

rows.title: Mapping Indigenous History Responsibly
rows.summary: How the map uses broad, overlapping evidence without presenting incomplete colonial records as fixed Indigenous borders.
rows.why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Published a new public education guide with 3 source-based answers.

rows.title: Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn
rows.summary: Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn (1847–1937) was a Shinnecock woman whose life connected language-bearing family knowledge, maritime labor, survival after the Circassian disaster, education, and intergenerational community continuity.
rows.why_this_matters: Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn’s life centers the work Shinnecock women carried through maritime loss: sustaining families, educating children, protecting kinship, and refusing the false claim that catastrophe made the community disappear.
rows.activity_update_summary: Expanded Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn’s biography with sourced family history, the Circassian loss, Shinnecock women’s continuity, a 1915 powwow photograph, and new mapped Historic Moments.

rows.title: Mary Rebecca Bunn (Aunt Becky)
rows.summary: Mary Rebecca Bunn, remembered as Aunt Becky, was a Shinnecock teacher, elder, and keeper of community memory. She is remembered in connection with the Shinnecock schoolhouse, family history, whaling knowledge, and twentieth-century community continuity.
rows.why_this_matters: Mary Rebecca Bunn's biography keeps Shinnecock women's education, family history, and elder memory visible. Her life helps connect reservation school history with broader Shinnecock community continuity across the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
rows.activity_update_summary: Expanded Mary Rebecca Bunn's biography with Hunter's family account and additional Shinnecock community context.

rows.title: Merrick People in Early Land Records
rows.summary: The history preserves Indigenous names that appear in early records connected with Merrick/Mericock, Massapequa, Rockaway, Hempstead, and neighboring western Long Island communities. Some people are represented by fuller biography pages because the references gives enough context. Others appear mainly as deed signers, witnesses, or named representatives, so their names are kept here without inventing life stories the records do not support.
rows.why_this_matters: The names of Merrick people in early land records preserve Indigenous presence, diplomacy, and memory while avoiding invented biography from thin evidence. Merrick Ancestral Land includes named Native people as well as places.

rows.title: Merrick and Freeport Indigenous Landscape
rows.summary: An overview of Meroke/Merrick and Freeport-area Native history, including south shore landscape context, archaeological evidence without sensitive locations, contact-period records, public markers, and modern acknowledgment.
rows.why_this_matters: Merrick and Freeport are part of a Native south shore homeland and a modern public-memory landscape. The place-name, deed, mission, marker, and exhibition records all point to histories that are still present, while vulnerable cultural places remain protected.

rows.title: Mocomanto, Shinnecock Sachem
rows.summary: Mocomanto was a mid-seventeenth-century Shinnecock leader named among the Native signers of the December 13, 1640 Southampton deed.
rows.why_this_matters: Mocomanto belongs in public Southampton history because English settlement narratives often obscure the Shinnecock leaders whose land, diplomacy, and signatures made those colonial records possible.

rows.title: Momoweta
rows.summary: Momoweta was a Corchaug sachem associated with the North Fork during the mid-seventeenth century.
rows.why_this_matters: Momoweta shows Corchaug leadership as active and diplomatic in the colonial record, while also revealing how much of Native leadership survives only through documents written by colonial authorities.

rows.title: Myth of Extinction and Native Survivance
rows.summary: Older claims that Long Island Native people no longer existed are misleading; Native communities maintained identity, kinship, culture, political action, and public presence into the present.

rows.title: Nasseconset, Sachem of the Nissequogue
rows.summary: Nasseconset, also written in variants such as Nassaconsett, Nasseconseke, Nasseconsack, Nesconsake, and Nassaskonsuk, was a Nissequogue sachem named in mid-seventeenth-century land records around the Nissequogue River and Smithtown.
rows.why_this_matters: Nasseconset connects the Nissequogue River and Smithtown area to a named Indigenous leader, while reminding visitors that deeds preserve only a narrow colonial view of Native authority.

rows.title: Nathan Jeffrey Cuffee
rows.summary: Nathan Jeffrey Cuffee was a Montaukett author, folk historian, and tribal-rights advocate associated with the Eastville community in Sag Harbor. He co-authored the 1905 historical novel Lords of the Soil with Lydia Jocelyn and helped carry Montaukett memory and land-rights advocacy into public record.
rows.why_this_matters: Nathan Jeffrey Cuffee connects Montaukett literary history with land-rights activism. His work as an author, folk historian, and advocate shows that Montaukett people continued to organize, write, and assert community rights in public long after colonial dispossession.

rows.title: Native Communities and the 'Thirteen Tribes' Model
rows.summary: Long Island's Native history cannot be reduced to thirteen fixed territories. Community names, place names, kinship, movement, diplomacy, and continuing nationhood reveal a more connected and changing political landscape.
rows.why_this_matters: The familiar map of thirteen fixed tribes can make colonial categories look older and more certain than they are. Reading names and boundaries critically makes room for Native kinship, mobility, political choice, and the continuing authority of present-day communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added 2 public education questions with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Native Long Island Overview
rows.summary: A public starting point for learning Native Long Island history through community continuity, land relationships, language, ecology, maritime labor, dispossession, sovereignty, and stewardship.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added 2 public education questions with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Native Plants
rows.summary: Native plant and environmental vocabulary connects Long Island plant life with recorded Indigenous language, source context, careful identification, and safety guidance.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added Hunter's historical account of Shinnecock women's gardening, gathering, plant knowledge, and seasonal storage without presenting remedies as medical advice.

rows.title: Native Resistance and Activism on Long Island
rows.summary: Native Long Island communities have defended land, burial places, sovereignty, and public memory through petitions, occupations, legal action, protest, and coalition work.
rows.why_this_matters: These actions show Native Long Island as continuing political life: communities organizing, refusing erasure, protecting ancestors, and asserting sovereignty in public.

rows.title: Native Signers in Place-Name Deed Records
rows.summary: Many place-name studies preserve Indigenous land names through colonial deed language, but the people named in those same records can be easy to miss. The records gathered here show cases where a placename, deed boundary, treaty, or confirmation also names Native signers, sachems, witnesses, interpreters, or representatives. Nearby leaders are included only when the cited record names them.
rows.why_this_matters: Placenames become clearer when read alongside the Native people named in deed records, without unsupported guesses about who signed, translated, or represented a community.
rows.activity_update_summary: Corrected the Cataconacke signer entry with exact pages, clarified the chief-counselor wording, and linked Sasarataicko's biography.

rows.title: Ninigret, Eastern Niantic Sachem
rows.summary: Ninigret was an Eastern Niantic sachem whose power and diplomacy reached across Long Island Sound. His actions affected Long Island Native communities, especially the Montaukett, during a century shaped by intertribal diplomacy, warfare, colonial alliances, and pressure on Native land.
rows.why_this_matters: Ninigret's story shows that Native Long Island history was never isolated from the wider Native Northeast. His actions across Long Island Sound affected Montaukett leadership, Quashawam's life, and the diplomacy and violence surrounding seventeenth-century Native communities.

rows.title: Nunnowa
rows.summary: Nunnowa is a Shinnecock thanksgiving gathering connected with seasonal gratitude, community, winter ceremonies, and continuing cultural practice.

rows.title: Orient (Transitional) Period (1,300 – 1,000 BC)
rows.summary: Named after unique burial sites on the North Fork of eastern Long Island, the Orient culture was transitional into the Early Woodland stage. It made abundant use of stone cooking pots and limited use of pottery which usually reproduced the form of the soapstone vessel.

rows.title: Paucamp
rows.summary: Paucamp, also recorded as Paueumpt, was a Corchaug elder associated with the Peconic Bay and Occabauk / Aquebogue landscape. The surviving record is brief but valuable because it preserves Indigenous boundary knowledge in a colonial documentary setting.
rows.why_this_matters: Paucamp's brief testimony preserves Native knowledge of North Fork boundaries and waterways through a named Corchaug elder. Even short records like this can show how Indigenous people carried detailed geographic knowledge into colonial legal documents.

rows.title: Penhawitz, Sachem of the Canarsie
rows.summary: Penhawitz, also written Penhawis, was a seventeenth-century Indigenous leader associated with the Keshaechquereren and Canarsie world of western Long Island, in what is now Brooklyn.
rows.why_this_matters: Penhawitz places Canarsie and western Long Island within Indigenous homelands with named leaders, diplomacy, and colonial pressure, not only later Brooklyn neighborhoods.

rows.title: Peter John Cuffee
rows.summary: Peter John Cuffee, also remembered as Rev. Peter John or Peter John, was an eighteenth-century Native minister connected with Hay Ground, Wading River, Poospatuck, Islip, Canoe Place, and the Manor of St. George. His life belongs to an intergenerational history of Native Christian leadership that later included his grandson, Rev. Paul Cuffee.
rows.why_this_matters: Peter John Cuffee's life connects Native-led religious work, education, and intergenerational ministry on Long Island before Rev. Paul Cuffee.

rows.title: Phase I Archaeology Investigation
rows.summary: A plain-language overview of Phase I Cultural Resource Investigations, what they are meant to identify, and why Native cultural and sacred areas require careful review.

rows.title: Phase II Archaeology Investigation
rows.summary: Phase II archaeological investigation is conducted in order to test or evaluate an archaeological site's eligibility for inclusion in the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP).

rows.title: Phase III Archaeological Investigation
rows.summary: Phase III archaeological data recovery gathers information from a site when preservation in place is not possible or when research questions require fuller excavation.

rows.title: Poggatacut, Sachem of the Manhassets of Shelter Island
rows.summary: Poggatacut was a Manhanset sachem associated with Shelter Island in the early contact period. Records and later histories connect him with Shelter Island, Gardiners Island, East Hampton, and Montauk, and preserve several spellings and related names, including Youghco, Yokee, Yovawan, and Pogaticut.
rows.why_this_matters: Poggatacut keeps Manhanset leadership visible in Shelter Island history. His appearances in early records show Native diplomacy and land relationships before town histories narrowed the story to colonial settlement.

rows.title: Post-contact – Present 1614 AD and Beyond
rows.summary: The post-contact period on Long Island includes land negotiations, colonial pressure, missionization, labor changes, debt, adaptation, and continuing Native resistance.

rows.title: Powwow
rows.summary: Powwow gatherings bring Native nations together through ceremony, social connection, cultural continuity, and contemporary community life.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Princess Sun Tama / Ann Harding Murdock
rows.summary: Princess Sun Tama, also known as Ann Harding Murdock, was an elected Matinecock spokesperson whose work connected community organization, land-rights advocacy, political representation, and continuing Matinecock presence.
rows.why_this_matters: Princess Sun Tama’s leadership shows Matinecock political life continuing through community organization, public testimony, land-rights advocacy, and demands for municipal recognition in the twentieth century.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a broader source-supported biography of Princess Sun Tama, including the 1958 Douglaston gathering, her election as Matinecock spokesperson, the 1969 Huntington letter and delegation, succession, and mapped Historic Moments.

rows.title: Projectile Points
rows.summary: Projectile points preserve thousands of years of Indigenous skill, hunting technology, stone knowledge, movement, and exchange. Many pointed stone tools commonly called arrowheads were made for spears or atlatl darts rather than arrows.
rows.why_this_matters: Projectile points are evidence of Indigenous engineering and knowledge across many generations. Reading them carefully avoids collapsing thousands of years of changing technology into the single modern label “arrowhead.”

rows.title: Quashawam
rows.summary: Quashawam was a Montaukett Sunksquaw whose life unfolded during warfare, succession struggles, and colonial land pressure in the seventeenth century. As a daughter of Wyandanch and Wuchikittawbut, she carried Montaukett authority through diplomacy, court orders, testimony, and land transactions from Montauk and Shinnecock country to Jamaica and colonial courts.
rows.why_this_matters: Quashawam makes Native women's leadership visible in Long Island records that are often told only through male sachems and colonial deed makers. Her biography also shows how colonial governments tried to simplify Native authority for land transactions, while Native kinship, diplomacy, and community responsibility were more complex.

rows.title: Raseokan / Ratiocan of Matinecock
rows.summary: Raseokan, also written Raseocan, Ratiocan, Rasaocume, Rashaokan, Resorokon, Aseton, Asiapum, or Asharoken in different records and later histories, was a seventeenth-century Matinecock sagamore associated with the North Shore around Huntington, Eaton's Neck, Cold Spring Harbor, Northport, Lloyd Neck, and Oyster Bay.
rows.why_this_matters: Raseokan / Ratiocan offers a glimpse of Matinecock leadership through the surviving record of North Shore land negotiations, while also showing the limits of colonial documents that preserve transactions more fully than personal lives.

rows.title: Researching Indigenous Long Island History Responsibly
rows.summary: How to use deeds, archives, archaeology, and community knowledge without trespassing or exposing sensitive places.
rows.why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Published a new public education guide with 1 source-based answer.

rows.title: Rev. Paul Cuffee
rows.summary: Rev. Paul Cuffee (1757-1812) was a Native Congregational minister born into Shinnecock and Unkechaug-connected family networks in Brookhaven. After early life in Wading River, he was ordained at Poospatuck in 1790 and traveled a preaching circuit that connected Wading River, Poospatuck, Islip, Canoe Place, Shinnecock, and Montauk. His life reflects Native-led ministry, kinship, travel, and community continuity across Long Island during a period of colonial pressure and change.
rows.why_this_matters: Rev. Paul Cuffee shows Native-led ministry, travel, education, and community continuity across Shinnecock, Unkechaug, Montaukett, and related Long Island Native communities.

rows.title: Sachem Aquash of the Montaukett
rows.summary: Aquash, also written Aquaas or Aquosh, was a late seventeenth-century Montaukett sachem whose recorded leadership appears in East Hampton and Montaukett land records during a period of colonial pressure on Montaukett land. Montaukett land-record sources first identify the sachem as Aquaas in 1684, and in 1687 Aquaas appears to have taken the name of his great-grandfather Wyandanch in a deed context. His life is only partly visible through surviving documents, but those records place him in Montaukett leadership.
rows.why_this_matters: Aquash matters because even a brief record can show Montaukett leadership continuing after Wyandanch, Moshup, and other earlier sachems. His recorded name and the later use of Wyandanch show how colonial records preserved fragments of Native authority during land pressure and dispossession.

rows.title: Sachem Tackapousha
rows.summary: Tackapousha, also written Tackapausha or Takaposha in some source records, was a seventeenth-century Massapequa leader whose diplomacy connected Massapequa, Merrick/Mericock, Rockaway, Secatogue, Matinecock, Canarsie, Dutch, and English records across western Long Island.
rows.why_this_matters: Tackapousha places Merrick and western Long Island history within Native leadership, diplomacy, and contested land records. His deed and court appearances show that Native people were not passive figures in colonial deeds; they negotiated, challenged, and defended land relationships under pressure.

rows.title: Sachem Warawakmy of the Setauket
rows.summary: Warawakmy was a mid-seventeenth-century Setauket sachem named in the April 14, 1655 Setauket land deed.
rows.why_this_matters: Warawakmy places Setauket history within Native homelands and leadership before English town formation. His brief record should be named clearly without pretending colonial sources preserved a complete life story.

rows.title: Samson Occom
rows.summary: Samson Occom, also written Sampson Occum or Samson Occam, was a Mohegan minister, teacher, writer, and Native political leader whose life connected Mohegan, Montaukett, Shinnecock, Oneida, and Brothertown histories.
rows.why_this_matters: Occom shows Indigenous intellectual leadership and community-building across regional boundaries. His story connects Long Island Native history with education, religion, writing, migration, and Native-led survivance.

rows.title: Sasarataicko (Sassakataka)
rows.summary: Sasarataicko, also recorded as Sassakataka and Sakkatakka, appears in seventeenth-century records as an advisor involved in marking Cataconacke boundaries; Gaynell Stone later connected him with a Montaukett co-sachem recorded in 1702–1703.
rows.why_this_matters: Sasarataicko's record shows Native governance through councils, boundary knowledge, succession, and negotiations over land—not only through a single famous leader. Reading the spelling variants carefully also shows why source transparency matters: later historians connect the early advisor and later co-sachem, but the original documents do not make every identity link explicit.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography and four linked Historic Moments distinguishing Sasarataicko's Cataconacke boundary role from later reconstructed identity links and a separate, uncertain whaling-register name.

rows.title: Shell Midden
rows.summary: Shell middens hold archaeological evidence of coastal foodways, village life, and environmental knowledge. They should be interpreted through broad landscape context and community care, with respect for community privacy and cultural protection.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Shinnecock Veterans and Wartime Service
rows.summary: Shinnecock military service spans multiple American wars and remains part of community remembrance, family history, and public memorial traditions.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added Hunter’s dated World War I Armistice account and World War II Selective Service context while keeping individual service details source-qualified.

rows.title: Slavery
rows.summary: Slavery on Long Island included African and Native labor under Dutch and English colonial systems, with Shelter Island and Suffolk County records preserving key evidence.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Sovereignty, Recognition, and Detribalization
rows.summary: Federal recognition, state recognition, reservation governance, and court decisions have shaped how Native political existence on Long Island has been affirmed, challenged, or denied.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Spring
rows.summary: Spring was a season of renewal and movement. As the weather warmed, families could shift from more protected winter places toward fields, streams, bays, and other seasonal work areas. Spring fish runs brought alewives, shad, striped bass, and other fish into freshwater streams, while early plant foods and new growth marked changes in the year.

rows.title: Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah
rows.summary: Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah, also remembered as Stephen Talkhouse, was a Montaukett man whose nineteenth-century life connects Molly's Hill in Springs, Montaukett homelands at Montauk, whaling and Civil War service, long-distance walking routes, and public memory of Montaukett survivance.
rows.why_this_matters: Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah is often remembered through walking legends, but the fuller cited sources connect those stories to Montaukett labor, military service, dispossession, Freetown community history, and public memory. The corrected timeline separates documented places from later path lore, making clear what is known, what is approximate, and what should not be overstated.

rows.title: Summer
rows.summary: Summer on Native Long Island centered on coastal abundance, shellfish harvesting, fishing, berry gathering, and the steady tending of gardens.

rows.title: Sunksqua Weany
rows.summary: Weany was a Shinnecock sunksquaw whose name appears in the April 1662 Quogue purchase record. The surviving colonial record preserves only a narrow view of her life, but it places her within Shinnecock leadership and land diplomacy in western Southampton during the seventeenth century.
rows.why_this_matters: Weany's record shows Indigenous women's leadership in land, law, and community sovereignty. Her presence makes visible a Shinnecock leader whose authority colonial histories too often reduce to a deed reference.

rows.title: Sunksquaws and Indigenous Women's Leadership
rows.summary: Native women belong at the center of Long Island history as leaders, diplomats, land authorities, culture keepers, workers, relatives, and community decision-makers.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Supporting Indigenous-Led Work on Long Island
rows.summary: Ways to support Indigenous-led organizations and knowledge holders without creating unpaid labor or competing projects.
rows.why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Published a new public education guide with 3 source-based answers.

rows.title: Sylvester Pharoah
rows.summary: Sylvester Pharoah was a nineteenth-century Montaukett leader, whaler, and recognized sachem or "King" in some source records. Sources connect him with Sag Harbor whaling records, his 1861 marriage to Jerusha Pharoah at Amagansett, and Montaukett life at Indian Fields before his death in 1870.
rows.why_this_matters: Sylvester Pharoah connects Montaukett leadership with labor history. His record helps show that nineteenth-century Montaukett life was not only a story of dispossession; it also included maritime work, family records, leadership, and continued claims to community land.

rows.title: Teaching Indigenous Long Island History
rows.summary: Teaching practices that connect Long Island history with living Native Nations and meaningful action.
rows.why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Published a new public education guide with 2 source-based answers.

rows.title: The Myth of the Thirteen Tribes
rows.summary: The familiar thirteen-tribes list is a useful clue in older sources but a misleading map of Native political life, kinship, and land relationships on Long Island.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: The Shinnecock Indians (1950): Book Guide
rows.summary: A chapter-by-chapter guide to Lois Marie Hunter’s 1950 Shinnecock-authored community history, connecting the book to related people, places, events, and research topics.
rows.activity_update_summary: Connected Hunter's foodways, plant knowledge, education, governance, ministry, powwow, and wartime-service chapters to their permanent articles and listings.

rows.title: Tribal Trustees
rows.summary: Shinnecock tribal trusteeship began under New York law in 1792, shaping community governance and lease records in the 1790s.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a public education question with concise answers, context, and source references.

rows.title: Vandalism
rows.summary: Vandalism and desecration have damaged sacred, burial, historical, and archaeological places, making preservation and careful stewardship necessary.

rows.title: Visiting Indigenous-Led Spaces Respectfully
rows.summary: Practical guidance for visiting public Native-led spaces, events, museums, and cultural programs with care.
rows.why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
rows.activity_update_summary: Published a new public education guide with 3 source-based answers.

rows.title: Wampum
rows.summary: Wampum connects shell, water, craft, diplomacy, exchange, tribute, memory, and coastal Indigenous knowledge across Long Island and neighboring homelands.
rows.why_this_matters: Wampum carries Indigenous knowledge through shellwork, diplomacy, ceremony, memory, art, and relationships among communities. Colonial trade changed its economic role but did not define or erase its Native meanings.

rows.title: Western Long Island Native Communities
rows.summary: Canarsie, Rockaway, Matinecock, Manhasset, Massapequa, Merrick, and neighboring western Long Island communities were connected across land, water, kinship, and history rather than isolated map points.

rows.title: Wickham Cuffee
rows.summary: Wickham Cuffee (1826–1915) was a Shinnecock whaler, navigator, trustee, Presbyterian elder, basketmaker, farmer, and keeper of family and community knowledge.
rows.why_this_matters: Wickham Cuffee’s biography connects Shinnecock maritime expertise, land governance, language and architectural knowledge, craft, church life, and family memory while directly rejecting the false ‘last Indian’ framing imposed by outside writers.
rows.activity_update_summary: Expanded Wickham Cuffee’s biography with sourced whaling, trusteeship, language, architecture, craft, family history, and mapped Historic Moments.

rows.title: William Wallace Tooker
rows.summary: William Wallace Tooker documented Long Island placenames, early spellings, deeds, and local histories. His work is valuable for source context, while his translations are read carefully alongside later scholarship.

rows.title: Winter
rows.summary: Algonquian peoples of eastern Long Island lived within seasonal relationships to land, weather, food, and shelter. Before and during the early contact period, winter could shift village life toward more sheltered inland areas and shared food-storage places.

rows.title: Wobetom
rows.summary: Wobetom, also recorded as Awabeton, Wahpetum, Awaupetun, Webbeton, or Woboton, was a seventeenth-century Montaukett leader, cattle keeper, and whaler. Foster H. Saville connected the name Wobetom with East Hampton records, including a 1657 deed, a 1670 cattle-keeping agreement beyond Fort Pond, and a 1675 whaling agreement.
rows.why_this_matters: Wobetom makes visible Montaukett leadership and labor in seventeenth-century East Hampton records. His name appears across land, cattle, and whaling documents, showing that Native people were active participants in local economies even as colonial records narrowed how their lives were preserved.

rows.title: Woodland Period (c. 1000 BCE-1640 CE)
rows.summary: During the Woodland period, Long Island communities made pottery, cultivated plants, hunted, fished, gathered coastal foods, and developed technologies including the bow and arrow.

rows.title: Worison, Unkechaug Whaler
rows.summary: Worison appears in seventeenth-century Unkechaug whaling and land records under several spellings, including Waishone, Warishone, and Areshunk.
rows.why_this_matters: Worison makes visible Unkechaug maritime labor and expertise in seventeenth-century Long Island. His record connects land, kinship, and whaling at a time when Native people worked within and against colonial economic systems.

rows.title: Wuchikittawbut, Montaukett Sunksquaw
rows.summary: Wuchikittawbut, also written Wicchitaubit or Wuch-i-kit-tau-but, was a mid-seventeenth-century Montaukett sunksquaw, widow of Wyandanch, and mother of Wyancombone.
rows.why_this_matters: Wuchikittawbut centers Montaukett women's leadership. Her documented leadership shows that Native political authority was not only male and that shoreline, whaling, inheritance, and land rights were central to community survival.

rows.title: Wyandanch
rows.summary: Wyandanch was a seventeenth-century Montaukett sachem whose leadership appears across Long Island records of diplomacy, warfare, land negotiations, and alliance politics. His name is also written in several forms in colonial records, including Wanutaugh, Wantagh, Waugwany, and Wyandance.
rows.why_this_matters: Wyandanch places Merrick-related land records within a broader Indigenous diplomatic world. His presence in western Long Island negotiations shows how Native leaders worked across community lines while colonial governments pressured Native land relationships.
